newsitem.title: CHINA: HK handover symphony blends cello, bells and street.
newsitem.headline: HK handover symphony blends cello, bells and street.

text.p: Hong Kong's Philharmonic Orchestra celebrated the territory's return to Chinese rule with a world premiere on Friday of a symphony in which choirs and a solo cello blend with Chinese bells and raucous street sounds.

Chinese composer Tan Dun said the piece, written for the association that organised the official Hong Kong handover celebrations, was based on the themes of love and harmony and scenes from Hong Kong's seedy Temple Street night market.

"Symphony 1997 (Heaven Earth Mankind)", part of which is called "Opera in Temple Street", was composed for solo cello, a choir, an orchestra and 64 Chinese bells, in this case replicas of rusty, excavated gongs from China's Hunan province.

"Twenty-five hundred years ago people would never imagine people 2,500 years later would be playing these bells in Hong Kong," said the 39-year-old Tan, one of the mainland's most renowned composers, who now lives in New York.
The orchestra played excerpts from the symphony on Tuesday to mark the former British colony's return to China.
Every night on Temple Street, musicians sing and play Chinese stringed "er hu" and traditional drums, while ageing prostitutes lean in doorways.
"Temple Street at night is where true Hong Kong souls are," Tan said. "For one hundred years, people have gone there every night to sing out all their sadness and happiness.
"I've been to Temple Street three times with my equipment to record all the street opera sounds and their very human stories," the composer said.
If you walk close enough, you can hear fortune tellers quietly advising clients under dim oil lamps.

Step back, and their voices will be drowned out by a cacophony of Cantonese opera and the cries of hawkers pushing smuggled mobile phones, herbal medicines and relics of the territory's colonial past to tourists and locals.
Some palm-readers and astrologers charge up to HK$1,000 (US$130) for a consultation. Or you can talk to the birds...
Seekers after truth squat on a stool by a cage and ask questions. A bird nips out and picks one of the cards laid out in front of the cage and places it in a slot.
The bird's owner and "interpreter" then gives a florid readout of the seeker's future prospects, at the same time rewarding the bird with seeds.
"I want people in 2,500 years' time to hear the sounds of Temple Street," Tan said.
